extracted.intended_audience: news consumers and news organizations (readers seeking trustworthy journalism, editors and journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: A checklist of eight trust indicators to evaluate the reliability, ethics, and transparency of news stories and news organizations. Each indicator explains what to look for and offers specific 'questions to ask' to judge trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you know who’s behind the news? If a journalist’s organization has rules they must follow to make sure their reporting is independent, accurate and honest, then their news will be more trustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Does the site use guidelines to protect honest and independent reporting? What is the site’s mission and priorities? Who funds them? (Look for organization-level policies, editorial standards, disclosures of mission and funding.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist Expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Who made this? We rely on the journalist’s knowledge because we are rarely present for events; journalists should follow strict standards for gathering solid evidence and multiple perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Are the journalist(s) credentials easily available? Do they have a good professional reputation as a journalist? Are they reporting on a topic or community they know well? (Look for bylines, bios, beats, credentials, and relevant experience.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels
rubrics_metrics.description: News? Opinion? Or what? Stories should be clearly labeled if they are designed to persuade; journalism should be clearly identified so readers know whether content is impartial or advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Is the story impartial or does it have a clear opinion? Is it highly partisan, sponsored or advertising something? Is the purpose clearly shown? (Check for clear labels like News, Opinion, Analysis, Sponsored, etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: References
rubrics_metrics.description: What’s their source? Journalists use eye witnesses, documents and other sources; when sources are shown, readers can check reliability themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: For investigative, in-depth or controversial stories, does the journalist provide sources for each claim? Do they give details so we can check the sources ourselves? Do other sources back up what is being said? (Look for named sources, documents, links, data, and corroboration.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: How was it built? Knowing why a journalist chose a story and how they reported it helps interpret whether the story is fast-moving, well-researched or impartial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: How much reporting was done? What methods were used? Who else was involved in the process? (Look for explanations of reporting methods, data collection, interviews, timelines, fact-checking processes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally Sourced
rubrics_metrics.description: Do they know you? Your community? Journalists who know and live in the community can explain events more sensitively and accurately; outsiders can improve reporting by engaging local knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Was the reporting done with deep knowledge about the local situation or community? Was the journalist on the scene? Did the journalist make an effort to listen to members of the community? (Look for local bylines, on-scene reporting, engagement with community sources.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Diverse Voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Who’s in the news? Who’s missing? If certain voices or experiences are missing, the coverage will be incomplete; look for inclusion of voices often marginalized by race, class, generation, gender, sexual orientation, ideology or region.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Does the newsroom commit to bringing in diverse perspectives? Is there evidence that the journalist pays attention to diversity? Are many types of communities represented accurately and fully? Are some completely missing? (Assess source diversity and representation in coverage.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Actionable Feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Does this news site listen to me? Inviting and listening to public feedback helps journalists ensure accuracy and completeness and can surface overlooked stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions to Ask: Does the news site invite the public to participate? Do they ask for feedback? Do they correct errors quickly, clearly and prominently? (Look for contact/feedback channels, correction policies, visible corrections and responsiveness to readers.)
